Again right now, this manhunt underway here in Berlin, here in Germany. And one of the things that we've been seeing here in the city is choppers overhead seemingly searching for someone. I've also seen several areas cordoned off with police vehicles and seemingly police officers also searching several places, including some of the subway stations here in Berlin.

So this is definitely a manhunt that's going on and full speed. And at the same time, as you can imagine, deep shock here in Berlin, deep shock here also among politicians in Germany as well, Victor.

BLACKWELL: Fred Pleitgen reporting there for us. Fred, thanks so much.

More than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes in southwest France. Firefighters are battling wildfires. Around 30 of them are burning right now. French officials say nearly a quarter million acres have already burned. Homes and cars are burned out shells as crews are working around the clock to try to keep those flames from spreading. About 7,000 people are now staying in temporary shelters, and a lot of them woke up to emergency alerts telling them to leave immediately and take whatever they could grab.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE (through translation): It's actually not knowing why we're really here, whether it's because of the fire approaching our home or the ashes that fell from the sky when the wind picked up and not knowing in the end when we'll be able to go home.

BLACKWELL: CNN's Melissa Bell joins us now from France. Melissa, last hour we saw you, you were near some of the smoldering remains of an area where the fire had already passed through. Where are you now?

MELISSA BELL, CNN SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: This is the command and control center to the south of this main fire from which the firefighters are coordinating their efforts, Victor, to try and get it under control. The trouble is that what happened last night is that the conditions got worse.

The fire, according to -- we've been hearing from the prime minister saying this morning, the very latest about what happened, the head of police as well and emergency services, the fact that what happened last night because of those conditions is that the fire started raging again uncontrollably with its own sort of wind systems and acting erratically and jumping from place to place.

So even as they'd managed to start containing it in those moments, places, I was just showing you a moment ago, Victor, where the fire started here on Wednesday, and still the embers smoldered, as you saw then, it continues to rage uncontrollably to the north of here. It is very large. There are several different centers to it. But now it has spread to the southeast. And that's why you've seen those extra evacuations overnight, 55,000 extra people evacuated overnight from their homes. And that fire now continuing to spread.

So the conditions extremely difficult here in terms of trying to bring this fire under control, even as they seek to contain it in one place. And that has not yet happened. It spreads elsewhere, and it is getting ever closer to Bordeaux city center. So extremely worrying situation on the ground. It is also extremely difficult for firefighters across the border, Victor.

In Spain, we've been looking these last couple of days at these wildfires to the west of Madrid. There had been some 60,000 evacuations as a result of those. Now it is the wildfires near Valencia that have been picking up with 15,000 fresh evacuations there.

And again, authorities really stretched to their limit. We were hearing only yesterday from the Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sanchez, about the fact that already yesterday 130,000 hectares had burned in Spain over the course of the year as a result of all these wildfires they've had. The annual average overall tends to be under 100,000.

So that gives you an idea of just how bad things are on both sides of this border as a result of this extremely hot summer and those conditions that have turned what we were just seeing here, the ground of these pine forests, the bracken and the ferns turned to kindling. So dry are they, Victor.

BLACKWELL: Melissa Bell reporting on the latest from these devastating wildfires there in France and Spain.

Maine Democrats, they've now chosen their nominee to run against incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins in November. This weekend, they selected former State Senate President Troy Jackson in a special convention to replace Graham Platner. Platner dropped out amid sexual assault allegations, which he's denied.

JACKSON: This is the absolute honor of my life to accept the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate.

Today, we turn the page. Today, this becomes a general election campaign. And today, we win the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.

BLACKWELL: CNN's Jeff Zeleny has more on how he won and what lies ahead for both candidates.

JEFF ZELENY, CNN CHIEF NATIONAL AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: Well, Maine Democrats finally turning the page in one of the most consequential Senate races in the country, formally replacing their Senate nominee. Of course, Graham Platner's campaign imploded a few weeks ago after months and months of controversy.

He was replaced by Troy Jackson, the former President of the Maine State Senate. He wasted no time going directly after his opponent, Republican Senator Susan Collins.

JACKSON: For nearly 30 years, Collins has told Maine that she is concerned. Maine does not need another six years of concern. We need someone with courage. We need a fighter. And we need a senator who remembers exactly who sent them to Washington, which is you.

ZELENY: Of course, Collins has a track record of winning in tough races again and again. Every Democrat who has tried to challenge her for 30 years has come up short. Of course, this is a different political environment. There is no question about that.

But for Jackson going forward, one thing is clear. He must unite his own Democratic Party, as well as make this a referendum on Senator Collins. But it's clear talking to delegates here, there's still some work to do to unite Democrats and move away from that Platner controversy.

We caught up with Jackson afterward and asked him about that.

ZELENY: Part of seeing the energy that Graham Platner brought without being consumed by the baggage, how do you do that?

JACKSON: Graham just tapped into, I believe, what was already there, people's frustration, you know, their anger that government was not working for him. This is not about Graham, it's about the movement, the people, the issues. It's bigger than any one person. I know for a fact it's bigger than me.

ZELENY: And as we talked to Jackson, he also told us that he would not support Chuck Schumer to be the Democratic Senate leader should Democrats win a majority in the U.S. Senate. But, of course, before any of that can be discussed, he must win this race. And that definitely remains an open question.

He said it is a challenge. There is no question about it, a fundraising challenge as well. Susan Collins has a big head start. The Democrats are all in on this race. They still see it as an important piece of the puzzle if they're going to try and win control of the Senate.

Jeff Zeleny, CNN, Bangor, Maine. BLACKWELL: Headlines we're watching this morning, a NASA astronaut is back on Earth after nearly eight months aboard the International Space Station. Chris Williams and two Russian crewmates landed safely in Kazakhstan about a half hour ago aboard the Soyuz spacecraft. It was the first space flight for Williams. He'll now begin post-landing medical checks before heading back to the U.S.

Gas prices climbing again as fighting between Iran and the U.S. intensifies. The average price for a gallon of gas is now $4.11 nationwide. That's up $0.11 in just the past week.

Renewed fighting has slowed shipping through key waterways in the Middle East, making it harder to move crude oil to world markets.

In New York, new video shows several teenagers riding on top of a moving subway train in Brooklyn. Look at this. Police say drones spotted six people on the train and alerted officers on the ground. Five teens were arrested, including a 12-year-old. Investigators say they recovered six stolen MTA keys from one of the suspects. The teens now face several charges, including reckless endangerment and criminal trespass.

Next, a high stakes meeting at the White House this week. What we can expect from the meeting between President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Plus, our panel reacts to President Trump ordering new signs at the Smithsonian Museum warning of, quote, "inaccurate information." That's coming up in the morning roundup.

BLACKWELL: This morning, CNN has new reporting about a key meeting related to the U.S. war with Iran. A source and U.S. officials say that Vice President JD Vance and Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine warned President Trump about potential consequences if he escalates the war. According to those sources, Caine expressed concerns about further depleting the U.S. munition stockpile and other possible negative effects.

Now, it's unclear if that's why the U.S. decided to suspend nearly two weeks of attacks against Iran. The U.S. military has conducted or rather continued its naval blockade of Iranian ports. U.S. Central Command posted on social media yesterday that it boarded a tanker in the Arabian Sea that violated that blockade.

CNN International Diplomatic Editor Nic Robertson is with us now. Nic, it's all happening ahead of that meeting between President Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their first since the start face-to-face in this war.

NIC ROBERTSON, CNN INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMATIC EDITOR: Yes, and it's going to be an important one because Prime Minister Netanyahu has not been happy with the ceasefire that was put in place several months ago, and it's not clear where he stands on the current pause that's underway at the moment. He was speaking to the government this morning.

He said that he'd be leaving for Washington tomorrow and that he would be meeting with President Trump on Tuesday, that all pending issues were going to be discussed, including Iran. So, I think everyone here imagines that's pretty much going to be front and center.

We've watched Omani diplomacy over the last couple of days. They took a trip, sent a delegation to Tehran. They got there Friday, left Saturday. The conversation was about the Strait of Hormuz. Of course, what the United States wants to see is Iran relinquish its desire and commitment to having some kind of payment method, some kind of continued control over ships coming and going from the Strait of Hormuz.

It's not clear if the Omanis made any headway there, but it perhaps was this sort of pause has allowed that diplomacy to happen. So the question is, how will the President view the outcome of the conversations the Omanis had?

But, as you say, the United States continuing its blockade. The Iranians doing the same, saying that they've stopped six ships from going into the Strait of Hormuz, not by fire, but they're saying those ships have been now put at anchor. But the U.S. Central Command saying that they have told 12 ships and stopped 12 ships from passing through the Strait of Hormuz over the last few days during the current bout of conflict.

So where it goes from here, this really does seem to be a matter of whether diplomacy has been able to take advantage of this pause.

BLACKWELL: Nic Robertson, thanks so much.

Question for you this morning, have you ever stuck around at a job you really didn't like? Well, more people are doing that. A new survey shows more than 20 million Americans are for the same reason. We'll tell you why coming up in the morning round up.

And let's take a look at Pittsburgh. Good morning.

BLACKWELL: New signage is going up outside the Smithsonian Museum, courtesy of the Trump administration. The signs warn visitors about, quote, "inaccurate information" in those exhibits.

Joining me now for the morning roundup, Jason "Jah" Lee, senior editor of Bossip, Atlanta News Anchor Kaitlyn Ross, and Attorney Madeleine Simmons. Everybody, welcome back to the table. We got some morning roundup veterans. Jah, let me start with you about this. This is an executive order the President signed on Friday, says that it warns the public of inaccurate information and then advises them or directs allegedly to other sources. What do you make of this being the continued narrative from the White House?

JASON "JAH" LEE, SENIOR EDITOR, "BOSSIP": It makes me feel like maybe Donald Trump and the administration, maybe they think they are like Tommy Lee Jones in "Men in Black." Like there's no special gadget that you can flash in front of our eyes. There's no sign that you can put up that will make us forget the history of America.

The history of America has always been, I guess, debated about what is being taught in schools and what kind of information people are taking in. But we all know generally what happened. And so to put this asterisk outside of somewhere like the Smithsonian that has a reputation of preserving that history and making sure that we're all aware of what's going on in the country, what has gone on in the country, it just -- it brings hollow to me as an effort to control a narrative that can't be controlled. The toothpaste is out of the tube.

KAITLYN ROSS, ATLANTA NEWS ANCHOR: The director of the Smithsonian really pushed back hard against this, saying that this is not a political exhibition, that they have sought to honor the history of the United States, and they do it very deliberately and with truth in mind. So I thought it was interesting just how strongly they pushed back against this.

MADELEINE SIMMONS, ATTORNEY: And the fact that, you know, the Trump administration can't get these signs inside of the Smithsonian --

SIMMONS: -- because they don't have any jurisdiction over that.

SIMMONS: -- but they can get them on the sidewalks, I think was a little bit funny because it just shows how petty it is. Like, you can't even get inside there to get this message out of the inaccurate information. You have to have it out on the sidewalk. So how impactful is that even going to be?

BLACKWELL: And that's one thing I wanted to ask you from a legal perspective. We saw what the White House tried to do at the Kennedy Center, right?

SIMMONS: Yes. Unsuccessfully.

BLACKWELL: Unsuccessfully. Is this something, you brought up jurisdiction inside the building, that even outside the building that somebody might be able to stop?

SIMMONS: So on the sidewalks -- BLACKWELL: Because the sidewalks are under the jurisdiction of the

Department of Interior.

SIMMONS: Right. I don't see them being able to stop putting signage on the sidewalks. But certainly, like at the Kennedy Center, trying to put signage on the actual building, they're not going to be able to do that.

BLACKWELL: Yes. You know, this is something, obviously, that the President has been focused on beyond the scope of the midterm elections. We've seen how culture war issues have impacted the vote. Is this going to be something people are thinking about in November? Do you think that the culture war element plays at all in the next 100 days?

ROSS: Well, I will say the reaction online is just as divided as we see people in person. People have very strong opinions about this, and it really is aligning with political values. So I think as you continue to see this fracturization and people go further and further to one side or the other, that's the reaction you're seeing to this.

So I think if you agree with it, you are screaming online that you agree with it. If you disagree, you are strongly in there with the exclamation points disagreeing. So it just depends what side you're on.

BLACKWELL: Kaitlyn, let me start with you on this next one. Elon Musk sat down with a reporter from The Economist. They talked about a lot, including his time as a special government employee and leading DOGE. Here's what he said.

ELON MUSK, BILLIONAIRE: I think I got a little too involved in politics, got carried away, frankly. So the, you know, the goal with the sort of DOGE stuff was to try to do something about the deficit, which is massive. So I thought, well, we need to sort of take a close look at spending and make sure that money is being spent in sensible ways and that it is not wasted or spent on fraudulent activities. And I got a lot of flack from this.

BLACKWELL: You covered the firings and layoffs here in Atlanta. CDC is here during the DOGE era where you know hundreds, thousands of people were losing their jobs. His takeaway is that he got the flack because he was thinking about sensible spending. Remind us of that period and just what it felt like for so many people.

KAITLYN ROSS, ATLANTA NEWS ANCHOR: Well, I think especially when we were covering government employees who, in their minds, they were being laid off from really essential positions. It's more than just getting carried away. My friends at the CDC were saying, we're taking away critical public health information that people need and it's keeping the community safe.

So, I think a little carried away might be an understatement here. And I thought it was interesting that he said it seemed almost to me in that clip like he was surprised that he got flack, but if you look at how strongly people feel about this it's surprising to me that he would be shocked by that.

JASON "JAH" LEE, SENIOR EDITOR, "BOSSIP": Well, Elon Musk has reportedly spent $250 million in support of the Trump campaign and the Trump administration. So. it just makes me wonder what is his definition of unnecessary spending? You know nowadays people have the public sentiment on billionaires and what it means to be a billionaire or trillionaire, in some people's cases, has turned.

And so, it just -- this is stuff that makes people kind of cringe at that whole concept, right, this guy was able to essentially donate his way into being a special government employee and then comes out after the fact and says, well, I didn't do that great of a job and maybe I was out of my depth. No kidding. You don't say.

But this is the kind of sugar honey iced tea that is made people upset about how people are hoarding wealth and what they're doing with it to control power.

BLACKWELL: I appreciate the morning translation there. Let's -- I want to talk about the Tate brothers in the couple of minutes we have left in this segment, Madeleine. These are two social media influencers known largely for their misogyny. They've been charged in the U.K. with several sex crimes including rape and sex trafficking. They've denied the allegations. What do we need to know about the parameters of this case?

MADELEINE SIMMONS, ATTORNEY AND PARTNER, STEWART MILLER SIMMONS: So, it's interesting with the Tate brothers because they were first charged in Romania. They were under house arrest there for three years. That case is ongoing for multiple sex trafficking type of charges. Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania to go to Florida. So, they flew to Florida on a private jet and have been in Florida since. And then the U.K., who already had some charges against them, came out with now a total of 59 charges together against both brothers for, like you said, very serious sex crimes. And so, they were able to effectuate that arrest in Florida, and now they're being held in a Florida jail.

The controversy is whether or not they'll be, you know, extradited to the U.K. Their lawyers would like them to stay here, of course, and they're trying to say, well, that may mess with the Romanian case, and it's not going to do that.

BLACKWELL: It's interesting because Andrew Tate is an outspoken Trump supporter and at least one of their attorneys is asking for the Trump administration to intervene. What do you think the likelihood of that is?

SIMMONS: I don't see the Trump administration intervening or the Department of State because there'd be no benefit to them to do that. It's a very normal process the treaty process between the US and the U.K. to extradite criminals in these types of situations. It is a legal process. You go before a judge. You show that the arrest was properly made, and I don't see this being as controversial as the Tate brothers would like it to be by getting politics involved. I think they're going to be on to the U.K. --

BLACKWELL: And politically, what benefit is there to the administration to intervene in a sex crimes case to keep these two men from going back to the U.K.?

SIMMONS: They have enough heat with the Epstein files. And if Marco Rubio is looking for a presidential bid he doesn't want to be involved with this.

BLACKWELL: Let's move on to this last one we teased before this segment. A new survey from West Health-Gallup Center on health care found that nearly a quarter of workers representing 23 million Americans they don't like the job they're in but they're staying just to keep the health insurance.

I mean, in one way this is a commentary on the expense of health insurance in this country and the difficult decisions people have to make.

ROSS: I mean, good benefits really are priceless. If you can go to the doctor if you can be seen for all of your needs that touches every aspect of your life, and to have to walk away from that is really difficult especially when you know that you have the stability and then you're looking at other jobs which maybe don't offer as good of a benefits package or they don't have that health insurance that you need. And so, it's understandable that people would stay in those situations.

LEE: And I would say also commentary on just livable wage and what money means and inflation and everything else. I mean, to stay somewhere where you are not particularly happy you maybe don't see professional growth there but to stay there just in case you get sick then you know that you might lose your house or lose your car or, you know, in other -- have other negative impact by not being able to afford a trip to the doctor with this bad state of affairs.

BLACKWELL: I mean, it's not the first time that this survey has found that a large group of Americans are doing this but it is a much higher number than it has been in previous surveys.

All right. Everybody stay with me we got a lot to hit. Next, spud surplus. Why one city is literally begging people to take 21 tons of potatoes off their hands.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK) [07:40:00]

BLACKWELL: ESPN just made some major cuts, the most dramatic of which happened mid-show, according to The Athletic. NFL analyst, Ryan Clark, was on air for NFL Live on Monday and found out that he was cut during the show. He didn't finish the program.

We're back with the Morning Roundup. Jah, Kaitlyn and Madeleine are here. Jah, let me start with you. Ryan responded to this in an episode of his podcast, "The Pivot." I'm going to play just a small portion of what he said.

RYAN CLARK, FORMER NFL PLAYER: What I'm not going to defend is you standing up for Angel Reese and everybody being mad about the way you did it, about what you said about, I'm not going to defend that. No. I'm not going to defend you standing on 10 toes for them all the time. It's not what I'm going to do. I'm not going to take those calls. And that was the decision that was made. And I believe that that has a large role in why it was made.

BLACKWELL: Yes. Clark there says that he believes that was the perspective of the bosses, that they would stand up for lawsuits and talent attacking executives, but they wouldn't stand up for him and his defense of Angel Reese. What do you think about what happened?

LEE: I think that Ryan Clark got swept -- you know, earlier we talked about culture war and how that is affecting things. And I think Ryan Clark got swept up in some level of culture war retribution. The fact -- the reason he got fired during the segment is because an outlet called OutKick was contacting ESPN, threatening to leak this information.

How would OutKick get this information? Well, OutKick is owned by Fox News Corp and was established by a man named Clay Travis. And if you know, Clay Travis, you know, he is not a bleeding-heart liberal. And so, I feel that this was -- I feel like a lot of this was purposely done to embarrass Ryan Clark. And ESPN has taken a lot of heat for being a liberal bastion lately. And I feel like his bosses perhaps thought this was a time to push the other direction.

BLACKWELL: Yes. I'd watched much more of the podcast and I think people should go there. Because he said that he was sad that he started to change himself to keep his job and that he thought he was so good that he wouldn't be fired. There's a lesson in that for everybody.

BLACKWELL: For everybody.

BLACKWELL: Let's talk about something else, it's pretty controversial on Capitol Hill. And it is about daylight saving time.

ROSS: You're going there.

BLACKWELL: So, the president wants it to be permanent. The House passed a bill to make it p

Manhunt Underway After Van Rams Into Crowd At Berlin Pride Event; Sources: Vance, Caine Raised Concerns About Escalating The War In Iran; Wildfires In Southwest France Continue To Spread, Over 250,000 Evacuations; U.S. Military Officially Confirms Identity Of Soldier Killed During Iranian Strikes In Jordan; Gas Prices Rise As Middle East Fighting Continues; President Trump Imposes New Tariffs Targeting Dozens Of Countries; Oil Supply Getting Cut Off At Two Crucial Points In Strait Of Hormuz; Maine Democrats Pick Jackson To Face Collins In November. Jackson Near Unanimous Choice As Maine Senate Candidate; Kalshi, Wisconsin Officials Clash Over Election Wagers; Massive Cyclosporiasis Outbreak Linked To Nine States; Colorado River's Two Big Lakes Hit Record Lows; More Than 70 Million Under Heat Alerts This Weekend; DC Prepares For Freedom 250 Grand Prix. Aired 6-7a ET

Aired July 26, 2026 - 06:00   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

VICTOR BLACKWELL, CNN ANCHOR: Welcome to CNN THIS MORNING. We are following several developing stories right now. Police in Berlin are on the hunt for a man they say purposefully rammed a van into a Pride event. At least one person has been killed. The latest on this is coming up in just a moment.

We're learning new details about the apparent pause in the U.S. bombing campaign in Iran. Could concerns about the U.S. weapons stockpile have something to do with that?

In Europe, hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated because these wildfires are raging in France and Spain. Extreme heat, the lack of rain are fueling the fires. We'll take you there live.

Plus, in this final sprint to the midterms, there's a warning for people who use prediction markets to bet on elections. How a law from the 1800s could impact your vote.

Brand new week. Let's start it off right. It's Sunday, July 26th. I'm glad to be with you. I'm Victor Blackwell.

Right now, there's a manhunt in Germany for the suspect who drove into a crowd at a Berlin Pride event. Berlin police say it's 21-year-old Abdul B. He killed one person, injured more than a dozen others late last night.

Police evacuated thousands of people from the event. Authorities say that the suspect used a white van to ram into people on the sidelines of the largest LGBTQ celebration in Germany's capital. An eyewitness describes the chaotic scene. Watch. (BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

UNIDENTIFIED ATTENDEE (through translator): At first, we couldn't make out what the screams were because of the party, the music and the atmosphere. And we only realized later exactly what was going on when the police cleared the park with machine guns and asked us to go home.

BLACKWELL: The van was later found abandoned after having crashed into a tree. CNN has asked Berlin police if this incident is being treated as an act of terror, and they say that, yes, this is being investigated as a suspected terror attack. Just getting that update.

We have new reporting this morning on the U.S. war in Iran. It involves a key meeting that President Trump had on Friday. Now, a source and U.S. official tell CNN that Vice President JD Vance and Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine came to warn President Trump at a meeting about escalating the war. The sources say that Caine told Trump his military options, but he also expressed concerns about further depleting the U.S. munitions stockpile and other possible negative consequences.

Now, it's unclear if those reasons prompted the U.S. to pause what had been nearly two consecutive weeks of strikes on Iran. The U.S. military has continued its naval blockade, though, of Iranian ports. U.S. Central Command posted on social media yesterday that it boarded a tanker in the Arabian Sea that violated that blockade.

Let's go now to CNN international diplomatic editor Nic Robertson. What is the Trump administration saying about the concerns of escalation ahead of this meeting with Netanyahu on Tuesday?

NIC ROBERTSON, CNN INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMATIC EDITOR: Yes. The concern is this is something that analysts, CNN, have spoken to as well have said that the defensive missile systems like the THAAD, the Patriot, a lot of them were used up defending against all those incoming Iranian missiles in the earlier part of the war a few months ago. So, that's a concern.

Significant number of Tomahawks also an attack -- land attack weapon also used up. So if you commit more weapon systems to another round of fighting, then you reduce your options for another war or another conflict in another theater around the world. That was from what we understand was the -- was the concern raised.

What it has allowed this pause, whatever the reason, and diplomats I'm talking to are sort of referring to this as an unannounced ceasefire, if you will, that's now gone through two nights, it's given an opportunity for an Omani delegation to go to Tehran. They went Friday, stayed into Saturday, left late Saturday to have conversations.

The Iranian foreign minister saying that there was progress in those talks, that they focused on the Strait of Hormuz. But there's absolutely no indication here whatsoever that the Iranians have given ground on their core point on the Strait of Hormuz, which is they want to have control over it and be able to make money out of it in the future.

The Iranians also have spoken about how they've caused a number of vessels, six vessels, to go to anchor and not transit the Strait of Hormuz. I think when you step back just a tiny little bit and look at the messaging from both the U.S. side and the Iranian side, both operate in their blockades, but not signaling it through maximalist shooting of ships but sort of one tempo down, if you will, the boarding and inspection and the ships being put at anchor.

Can this pause for diplomacy hold? And as discussed here, the cost of an escalation, there are implications with that. And that was what was explained to the president.

BLACKWELL: All right. And we'll check the trajectory, of course, after this meeting at the White House on Tuesday. Nic Robertson, thank you so much.

More now than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes in southwestern France. Firefighters are battling dozens of wildfires, about 30 fires are burning right now.

French officials say that nearly a quarter million acres have burned. Homes and cars are burned out shells. Crews are working around the clock to try to keep the flames from spreading. Thousands of people now say they have to stay in temporary shelters, and many of them woke up to emergency alerts telling them to leave immediately with whatever they could carry.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE (through translator): Evacuating 200,000 people, that's never been seen in France, never. Not since the war have we seen anything like this. Even the worst disasters that have happened, this has never occurred.

BLACKWELL: CNN's Melissa Bell is joining us now from France. Melissa, what are you seeing this morning?

MELISSA BELL, CNN SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Well, this is the part of France where the fire, this main fire that continues to spread and has not yet been contained, the Gironde fire, as it's being called, started. This was on the night from Wednesday to Thursday. Four days later, you can see how dangerous it still is.

What we've been watching over the course of the last couple of hours that we've been standing here, is this very dry ground through which the fire had passed, but is no longer active you still have these smoldering embers underneath the pine trees. And it's an indication not just of how flammable this kind of vegetation is, the pine trees, but also the ferns that have acted as a kind of kindling given how dry it is. But also the fact that once -- even once we're outside of the perimeter where the fire is actively burning and the flames are very high, it picks up again.

Again, it was four days ago that the fire spread through here. And still, what we've been seeing over the last hour or so, we've been here, are civilians going around with water on their trucks to try and get these sort of starts of fire themselves, even as the main firefighters, all 1,500 of them continue to battle the actual fire itself, which has overnight because the conditions slightly windy spread much, much further to the south and east.

In fact, what we saw overnight were 55,000 more people evacuated from their homes, which brings to the whole Gironde region over the course of the last couple of days, 220,000 people evacuated and currently living in the kind of shelters we visited last night in Bordeaux. People sleeping on cots with their families, elderly people who've been evacuated from residential homes and none of them any idea yet of when they might be able to get home.

On the contrary, more and more villages being evacuated, the fire continuing to spread. It has now burned 42,000 hectares. Just like this. This pine forest of the southwest of France, a million hectares of it that spread to Spain. And this monoculture, of course, that in these very dry conditions we've seen here in France this summer, these excessive heat waves, these record breaking temperatures, once it gets hot down here and the fire start, they are very, very difficult to stop, Victor.

BLACKWELL: Yes. It's remarkable how you say that the firefighters are really trying to get those active fires under control. And it's just the everyday citizen going around to spaces where you are trying to douse any of those embers that we know from here in the U.S. can pick up and be moved and cause a greater fire somewhere else. Melissa Bell, thanks so much for the reporting. We'll check back.

Authorities in Spain say that wildfires there have now killed at least one person. More than 100,000 acres have burned near the Spanish capital of Madrid. Ninety thousand people have been forced to leave or take shelter elsewhere. One evacuee described the moment that she realized it was time to go.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE (through translator): I saw clouds of smoke rising into the sky. That's when I realized something was happening. I think we all panicked. Then we received the message telling us to get ready, take whatever valuables we could. Whatever was most important. I took my cat and we left.

BLACKWELL: Hundreds of firefighters are working to keep two major wildfires west of the capital from merging into an even larger fire.

The Pentagon has officially identified one of the service members killed in this month's Iranian strike on a base in Jordan. Officials say staff Sergeant Angel Rampersad, a 28-year-old from New York, was among those killed in the July 17th attack. Officials had previously said they believed that she was one of the victims. They have now formally confirmed her identity after positive identification by military examiners.

Gas prices starting to climb again as fighting between Iran and the U.S. intensifies. The average price for a gallon of gas is now at $4.11 across the country. That's up $0.11 in just the past week.

Renewed fighting has slowed shipping through key waterways in the Middle East, making it harder to move crude oil to world markets. While the tariff time out that's ended despite a Supreme Court ruling, dozens of U.S. trading partners are now being forced to pay up. We'll explain the impacts of these growing tariffs.

Plus, Democrats in Maine named their new Senate nominee in the race to unseat Senator Susan Collins in November. We'll hear from that new candidate.

Also, the green flag will drop D.C. -- drop in D.C. next month for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix. We'll show you our tour of the 1.7 mile course that wraps around the National Mall.

BLACKWELL: A new round of tariffs just kicked in on almost every single U.S. import. Here's why. The U.S. claims that 60 of its trading partners are using forced labor to produce goods exported to the U.S. These tariffs hit Friday just after another similar tariff expired.

So while it won't hit your wallet too much, rising gas prices will. We'll talk about that, of course, all the factors that have prevented oil from surging recently are either weaker or gone.

I'm joined now by Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance, Ben Werschkul. Ben, welcome back to the show. Let's start with the tariffs.

The tariffs have been unpopular here across the U.S. since so-called Liberation Day. While these tariffs are not nearly as high as the ones implemented that were shut down by the Supreme Court, you've got reporting about the impact and how much it's really going to affect the imports coming in from around the world.

BEN WERSCHKUL, WASHINGTON CORRESPONDENT, YAHOO FINANCE: Yes, yes. Good to be with you. These tariffs are, as you mentioned, these tariffs are kind of a changeover of sorts to new tariff authorities that aren't going to have a lot of impacts immediately. But there is a lot of evidence here that what Trump is trying to do is set up more tariffs down the road as he goes forward.

The main -- the main headline this week was a switch up of tariffs from 10 percent tariffs that expired on Friday at midnight to new tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent that came into effect at 12:01. So just one minute later on this issue of forced labor, you mentioned here.

This doesn't change the tariff rate, but it does create a more legally durable option that the White House thinks they can build on. We're expecting more investigations there in the months ahead that could that could raise these rates even as they don't change now.

Another important strand on tariffs to watch this week is Trump's announcement on Canada. He talked about 50 percent tariffs on Canada that could be in effect by August on some goods. This again has sort of limited immediate effects. It's only import -- impacts about five percent of U.S. imports. But this is a new tariff authority that Trump -- that we haven't seen from Trump before.

He's reaching all the way back to the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 for this. This is a much more legal -- much more quick acting option that has a lot of legal problems. The question whether this stands up in court is a big one. But the sense I get from listening to the administration and talking to trade officials is that they're trying to see if this will stick. If this will stand up in court and if Trump can do this, he could -- we could see a lot more from that in the months ahead.

But the bottom line, as you mentioned, tariff rates began this week at about 11 percent. They're still at 11 percent. They're just trying to push it up higher to these kind of pre liberation -- or these Liberation Day rates.

BLACKWELL: We'll see if there's any retaliation. Of course, we saw that, excuse me, in 2025 from Canada, China, other countries as well. Let's talk about oil prices above $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May. This morning, as we've reported, $4.11 per gallon for regular nationally on average.

When you add in the Houthi's attacks on vessels passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, in addition to what's happening at the Strait of Hormuz. How does that change the prospect for the next several weeks or months of this war and the price of oil?

WERSCHKUL: Absolutely. No, it really creates a real level of uncertainty in the energy sector that is really notable. The third factor I'll add for you is the war in Ukraine. That is an underappreciated aspect of this with Russian refineries being bombarded here. So this is essentially a perfect storm for the energy sector and has seen crude oil prices up 20 percent over the last month.

And as you mentioned, prices at the pump 4.11. One important, I think, conversation amongst the sector is how things aren't worse on this 4.11 price. I don't want to downplay 4.11 a gallon of gas. That's lower than it was earlier in the war and it's lower than it was -- it was $5.00 a gallon of gas just a few years back.

This comes as the energy sector has talked about how things could get -- could get worse in a hurry here if inventory levels continue to drop as they're going forward. But there's also been predictions since February, since this war in Iran began, of much more dire consequences here than what we're seeing at moment.

Again, $100 a gallon for crude oil and $4.11 gas is significant, but there's a lot of folks out there that are thinking the inventory levels and things like demand could pick up in the weeks ahead and push things even worse. Bottom line here for oil markets is no one really knows what's going to happen. And we've had predictions for months now that have been -- that have been mixed on this front. But we are seeing pressure on a lot of different fronts from around the globe.

BLACKWELL: Speaking of predictions, and I got 30 seconds for you here, Ben, we've got a Fed meeting coming up midweek. What's the expectation on rates?

WERSCHKUL: Yes, all eyes will be on the Federal Reserve. The expectation is that rates will be steady. But we are going to have a real conversation at the Fed about all these different factors. Oil prices are a major one.

The new chairman, Kevin Warsh, has sort of taken the Fed out of the business of offering forward guidance here but they are expecting to keep rates steady. The question is when they have to step in on rates. For right now lower inflation -- lower inflation readings for June means the Fed probably holds steady, but they're likely to raise this fall is what the expectation is.

BLACKWELL: Ben Werschkul, thanks so much. Enjoy the week. And be sure to watch "STATE OF THE UNION" later this morning. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, White House Border Czar Tom Homan, and Louisiana Senator Bill Cassidy will be among the guests. That's at 9:00 a.m. eastern, right here on CNN.

Place your vote and not your bet. Why was Wisconsin election officials are using an old law from the 19th century to scare election gamblers away from the prediction markets.

And good morning to our friends in the beautiful Windy City. Sun's just coming up in Chicago.

BLACKWELL: Democrats in Maine formally tapped Troy Jackson this weekend as their U.S. Senate nominee. Jackson is a former state Senate president. He replaces Graham Platner on the ballot after Platner dropped out amid sexual assault allegations.

Jackson's nomination sets up a showdown with Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins in November. Democrats believe Maine is firmly in play and the race is considered a central battleground in their fight to get control of the Senate.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP) TROY JACKSON (D), MAINE SENATE NOMINEE: This is the absolute honor of my life to accept the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate.

Today, we turn the page. Today, this becomes a general election campaign. And today, we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.

BLACKWELL: Michael Shepherd joins us now. He's a reporter with the Bangor Daily News. Michael, good to have you.

All right. So, he replaces Graham Platner. Graham Platner, obviously, galvanized Democrats there in Maine in this showdown with Susan Collins. Troy Jackson he won all but five of the delegates at this convention. So, he had the people in the room. But outside of that room, how is he compare to his predecessor?

MICHAEL SHEPHERD, REPORTER, BANGOR DAILY NEWS: Yes, I think Troy Jackson is the best one to one comparison that Democrats could have made to Graham Platner, similar base, similar progressive stances, big in the labor movement. He was a guy who was campaigning with Graham Platner before. It was clear that Graham Platner was even going to beat Janet Mills in the primary, which seems like eons ago.

So I think in that sense, Democrats avoided sort of an ideological issue by substituting a candidate who's pretty similar to the guy that that was obviously knocked out of this race. He's a much different guy. He's 58 years old. He's been around for a long time in Maine politics. He kind of got famous up here when he and a few other loggers blockaded the Canadian -- part of the Canadian border over labor issues back in 1998, got elected to the legislature four years later and has kind of risen from a backbencher to the Senate presidency and to these very high profile campaigns.

Obviously, he's from northern Maine. He's got -- he's from a place where it's very socially conservative, had a lot of social conservative votes early in his career, anti-abortion, voted against gay marriage in 2009, was NRA endorsed, has kind of flipped on all those issues.

So he's got a story. I think a lot of Mainers understand on one hand, but it's a little hard to translate to the national level. And he's going to have to be explaining that to a lot of different people in a really quick amount of time.

BLACKWELL: You mentioned that previous anti-abortion stance. CNN's "KFILE" revealed his 2010 pro-life lawmaker survey, a questionnaire he filled out in which he said that he did not think that abortion should ever be legal, did not answer the questions about exceptions for rape, incest, life of the mother.

His campaign released this statement. In the years since these questionnaires, Troy listened to and learned from the women, doctors, and families across Maine, and evolved.

Unlike Susan Collins, who stripped millions of women of their constitutional rights by casting the decisive vote for justices who overturned Roe v. Wade. Has that created any problems with him in for in this race?

MICHAEL SHEPHERD, REPORTER, BANGOR DAILY NEWS: Well, I think it's just something he has to explain to a national audience. I think this is something that people in state understand a little bit. This is this is northern Maine. This is a much different cultural place than the rest of the state. There's a long history of Democrats up there who had these views. Also, it's a place now that's controlled by Republicans in the state legislature and everything else.

So, Troy Jackson's case here is that I have evolved and I have been able to win in places where other Democrats can't. I think this is obviously a big step up. And that part of the state is not so easily translatable to the rest of it. But I think there's a story here that he can tell. It's going to be on the voters and on the national folks who are also viewing this, how they're going to respond to it.

BLACKWELL: You've reported on the significant funding gap in this race. The Republicans have a larger bank than the Democratic candidate here. Does Jackson, does his campaign, do they seem to be concerned about the deficit?

SHEPHERD: I think they're not saying they're concerned. I think they've got to be concerned. Republicans have just stacked up an enormous amount of outside money in this race, multiple super PACs doing multiple different things for Susan Collins. There are ones that are attacking Democrats. There are ones that are running really positive ads on money that Collins has secured for fire stations and things like that.

So they're running a multi front war to set Susan Collins up. And the thing about Jackson is he's not historically a very good fundraiser. The good news for him is that you don't really have to be in this era of battleground races where the money just comes in and finds you.

So, I expect him to catch up to Susan Collins here. He said in less than a week. Right. He raised or the beginning of his campaign, he raised around a million dollars. He's obviously going to have to plus that up and be one of the bigger fundraisers on ActBlue.

But I think this will even up just because of the stakes of the race. It's just too big for Democrats to leave much on the table here.

BLACKWELL: Yes. And we saw that Chuck Schumer stayed out of the race there in Maine when Graham Platner was the nominee. We'll see if that changes as they get closer to Election Day there now that Troy Jackson is the Democratic nominee.

Michael Shepherd there. Thank you so much for your reporting.

High stakes showdown is unfolding in Wisconsin, where prediction market giant Kalshi is battling state officials over a centuries old law. The measure makes a felony to vote in any election you're also betting on.

CNN's Marshall Cohen has more for us.

MARSHALL COHEN, CNN SENIOR REPORTER: Well, you don't see this every day. And this war of words between Kalshi and election officials really highlights how the rapid expansion of prediction markets is scrambling the midterms.

So let me break down exactly what happened here. Earlier this week, the bipartisan Wisconsin Election Commission warned voters about an old state law from the 1800s that prohibits residents who bet on an election from casting a ballot in that same race.

The press release said, quote, if you bet on an election, it could cost you your vote. And they said voters could even face post-election challenges to their qualifications. And if proven, their ballots could be thrown out and offenders might be prosecuted.

Now, look, the officials were very clear that they aren't policing these prediction markets. They just wanted everybody to be aware, especially before anyone goes on social media later and brags about their winnings. But all of this caught the attention of Kalshi, which is the biggest prediction market in the country.

Company leaders went on the attack against Wisconsin election officials. Here's what one Kalshi employee posted, quote, this is insane. The commission is implying that they will literally disenfranchise voters. He went on to say not only is the commission statement illegal and dishonest, it's active voter suppression.

Now, look, it's absurd for them to claim that it's illegal to send a press release. I don't even know what that means. But the experts I spoke to did agree that there are some legitimate questions about whether this very old law is even enforceable or constitutional. And it's never a good look to possibly throw out someone's vote.

But it is clear from Kalshi's red hot reaction that they don't want anyone standing in the way of their booming business. Not even the public servants who run our elections. And these markets, in fact, are pretty darn popular. Kalshi has seen $30 million in trading volume so far on who will win the House and Senate this November.

And by the way, one last thing for full disclosure. CNN has a partnership with Kalshi. We use its data to cover major events, but editorial employees are prohibited from trading on prediction markets.

Marshall Cohen, CNN, Washington.

BLACKWELL: Nine states now have related cases of a diarrheal illness caused by cyclospora. This could turn out to be one of the largest outbreaks of foodborne illnesses in the U.S. in three decades.

Here's CNN's Jenn Sullivan.

JENN SULLIVAN, CNN REPORTER (voice-over): Cases of a diarrhea illness known as cyclosporiasis have risen drastically this summer. It's a gastrointestinal infection caused by a parasite.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It's transmitted by food and water.

SULLIVAN (voice-over): As of Friday, 41 states have reported at least one case this season, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But this specific outbreak is concentrated in the nine states listed on this map. Their health departments have reported over 12,000 cases of cyclosporiasis so far this summer. At least 98 people have been hospitalized, according to the CDC.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: This may be a more complicated set of outbreaks than simply just one with one source.

SULLIVAN (voice-over): Symptoms include explosive diarrhea, nausea, abdominal cramping, bloating and fatigue. And unlike a stomach bug that lasts 24 to 48 hours, symptoms of cyclosporiasis can last for weeks if untreated.

The Food and Drug Administration says the likely source linked to the nine state outbreak is shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms to Mexico. The company voluntarily recalled the product last week.

ROBERT F. KENNEDY JR., SECRETARY, HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES: We do have the outbreak under control. We have done extensive forensics, epidemiological forensics.

SULLIVAN (voice-over): But experts say symptoms of the illness can take up to two weeks, and the epidemiological curve of new cases hasn't yet slowed.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: It's going to be hard to sort this out for one of these major centralized distributors.

SULLIVAN (voice-over): The CDC recommends washing all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating, and notes washing alone cannot guarantee the parasite's removal.

But cooking can kill the parasite. Make sure you're not eating lettuce that has been recalled.

I'm Jenn Sullivan reporting.

BLACKWELL: Next, water levels at two of America's biggest reservoirs are at historic lows. Why experts are sounding the alarm.

And we're following breaking news this morning. An American astronaut and two Russian cosmonauts just touched down in Kazakhstan. They just wrapped up a 240-day -- 41-day mission aboard the International Space Station. We'll get you more of that.

And if you're heading out and you're thinking, I don't want to leave Victor yet, but I got to go. You can take me with you. You can stream the show from anywhere in the U.S., right from the CNN app. You can also go to CNN.com/Watch.

BLACKWELL: A lifeline for 40 million people is at risk this morning. The Colorado River is drying up. The crisis is reaching a critical new stage.

This month, two of the river's major reservoirs Lake Mead and Lake Powell dropped to their lowest levels on record. Seven states depend on the river for drinking water, agriculture, hydropower, it helps generate electricity for about 700,000 homes and irrigation -- irrigates rather more than 5 million acres of farmland across the southwest.

CNN's chief climate correspondent Bill Weir has more.

BILL WEIR, CNN CHIEF CLIMATE CORRESPONDENT: Well, much the way we're seeing record-shattering temperatures across the American West and Sout

VICTOR BLACKWELL, CNN HOST: Welcome back to CNN This Morning. Here's what you need to know. There is breaking news out of Germany. Police say a man intentionally ramped his car into a pride event in what they're calling an act of terror. We have a live report for you on that in a moment.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been forced to leave as wildfires rage in France and Spain. Extreme heat and the lack of rain are really fueling those fires. We'll take you there live.

And it's take two for Maine Democrats. They've nominated a new candidate to take on GOP Senator Susan Collins.

TROY JACKSON (D), MAINE SENATE NOMINEE: For nearly 30 years, Collins has told Maine that she is concerned. Maine does not need another six years of concern.

BLACKWELL: How Democrats are hoping to shift the focus back on Collins in this final sprint to the midterm election. The skies over Iran, again, quiet for a second night in a row as the U.S. pauses its bombing campaign there. Good concerns about the U.S. weapons stockpile be to blame.

Plus, did DOGE go too far?

Sunday, July 26th. Good to have you with me. I'm Victor Blackwell.

Right now, German police are searching for the suspect accused of a deadly terror attack at a Berlin Pride event. Berlin police say that one person is dead, 15 others are injured, some of them from stab wounds. Police have identified this man, 21-year-old Abdul B., as the person they say rammed into a crowd gathered for Germany's largest LGBTQ event. Now, authorities say the suspect hit several people with a white van that was later found abandoned after it slammed into a tree.

CNN Senior International Correspondent Fred Pleitgen is with us now. Fred, what's the latest?

FREDERIK PLEITGEN, CNN SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Good morning. And this is pretty much as close as we're going to be able to get to the scene of where all of this happened. We're about, I'd say, about 100 yards away from where that van slammed into a tree.

I'm going to get out of your way for a second. We're going to see if we can zoom in to where this happened. You can see the van there is still very much up against that tree. We've been seeing police forensic teams there working on that vehicle, but we can also see, we have seen from several angles here, that the van's front is completely totaled.

So certainly that meshes with some of the things that eyewitnesses have been saying, that apparently it went down that path at a pretty high velocity ramming into people. One of the things we need to point out is that area that you're seeing there, where that van is now standing up against that tree, that is not a public road. That is actually a path through one of the main parks here in the center of Berlin.

And eyewitnesses certainly say that that vehicle plowed through the crowd that was taking place here on the sidelines of that Pride event. And there were eyewitnesses who said that they were absolutely terrified by what was going on. Here's what one of them said.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE (through translation): At first, we couldn't make out what the screams were because of the party, the music and the atmosphere. And we only realized later exactly what was going on when the police cleared the park with machine guns and asked us to go home.

PLEITGEN: All of this happening, of course, on the sidelines of the big Christopher Street Day Pride event here in Berlin that was taking place on Saturday. And you're absolutely right to point out that the police have now launched this very public manhunt with an image of what they say is the main suspect in this ramming, Abdul B, 21 years old. They say he's about 6'3, has black hair.

And the police are urging anyone who sees him to actually dial the German version of 9/11, which is 110, rather than to try and talk to this person saying that he could be armed and could potentially be very dangerous. The police also coming out and saying that they believe that he was in the Islamic -- Islamist scene in Germany. Not exactly clear what that specifically means, but certainly saying that those seem to be some of the leanings that this person appears to have had.

Again right now, this manhunt underway here in Berlin, here in Germany. And one of the things that we've been seeing here in the city is choppers overhead seemingly searching for someone. I've also seen several areas cordoned off with police vehicles and seemingly police officers also searching several places, including some of the subway stations here in Berlin.

So this is definitely a manhunt that's going on and full speed. And at the same time, as you can imagine, deep shock here in Berlin, deep shock here also among politicians in Germany as well, Victor.

BLACKWELL: Fred Pleitgen reporting there for us. Fred, thanks so much.

More than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes in southwest France. Firefighters are battling wildfires. Around 30 of them are burning right now. French officials say nearly a quarter million acres have already burned. Homes and cars are burned out shells as crews are working around the clock to try to keep those flames from spreading. About 7,000 people are now staying in temporary shelters, and a lot of them woke up to emergency alerts telling them to leave immediately and take whatever they could grab.

UNIDENTIFIED FEMALE (through translation): It's actually not knowing why we're really here, whether it's because of the fire approaching our home or the ashes that fell from the sky when the wind picked up and not knowing in the end when we'll be able to go home.

BLACKWELL: CNN's Melissa Bell joins us now from France. Melissa, last hour we saw you, you were near some of the smoldering remains of an area where the fire had already passed through. Where are you now?

MELISSA BELL, CNN SENIOR INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: This is the command and control center to the south of this main fire from which the firefighters are coordinating their efforts, Victor, to try and get it under control. The trouble is that what happened last night is that the conditions got worse.

The fire, according to -- we've been hearing from the prime minister saying this morning, the very latest about what happened, the head of police as well and emergency services, the fact that what happened last night because of those conditions is that the fire started raging again uncontrollably with its own sort of wind systems and acting erratically and jumping from place to place.

So even as they'd managed to start containing it in those moments, places, I was just showing you a moment ago, Victor, where the fire started here on Wednesday, and still the embers smoldered, as you saw then, it continues to rage uncontrollably to the north of here. It is very large. There are several different centers to it. But now it has spread to the southeast. And that's why you've seen those extra evacuations overnight, 55,000 extra people evacuated overnight from their homes. And that fire now continuing to spread.

So the conditions extremely difficult here in terms of trying to bring this fire under control, even as they seek to contain it in one place. And that has not yet happened. It spreads elsewhere, and it is getting ever closer to Bordeaux city center. So extremely worrying situation on the ground. It is also extremely difficult for firefighters across the border, Victor.

In Spain, we've been looking these last couple of days at these wildfires to the west of Madrid. There had been some 60,000 evacuations as a result of those. Now it is the wildfires near Valencia that have been picking up with 15,000 fresh evacuations there.

And again, authorities really stretched to their limit. We were hearing only yesterday from the Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sanchez, about the fact that already yesterday 130,000 hectares had burned in Spain over the course of the year as a result of all these wildfires they've had. The annual average overall tends to be under 100,000.

So that gives you an idea of just how bad things are on both sides of this border as a result of this extremely hot summer and those conditions that have turned what we were just seeing here, the ground of these pine forests, the bracken and the ferns turned to kindling. So dry are they, Victor.

BLACKWELL: Melissa Bell reporting on the latest from these devastating wildfires there in France and Spain.

Maine Democrats, they've now chosen their nominee to run against incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins in November. This weekend, they selected former State Senate President Troy Jackson in a special convention to replace Graham Platner. Platner dropped out amid sexual assault allegations, which he's denied.

JACKSON: This is the absolute honor of my life to accept the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate.

Today, we turn the page. Today, this becomes a general election campaign. And today, we win the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.

BLACKWELL: CNN's Jeff Zeleny has more on how he won and what lies ahead for both candidates.

JEFF ZELENY, CNN CHIEF NATIONAL AFFAIRS CORRESPONDENT: Well, Maine Democrats finally turning the page in one of the most consequential Senate races in the country, formally replacing their Senate nominee. Of course, Graham Platner's campaign imploded a few weeks ago after months and months of controversy.

He was replaced by Troy Jackson, the former President of the Maine State Senate. He wasted no time going directly after his opponent, Republican Senator Susan Collins.

JACKSON: For nearly 30 years, Collins has told Maine that she is concerned. Maine does not need another six years of concern. We need someone with courage. We need a fighter. And we need a senator who remembers exactly who sent them to Washington, which is you.

ZELENY: Of course, Collins has a track record of winning in tough races again and again. Every Democrat who has tried to challenge her for 30 years has come up short. Of course, this is a different political environment. There is no question about that.

But for Jackson going forward, one thing is clear. He must unite his own Democratic Party, as well as make this a referendum on Senator Collins. But it's clear talking to delegates here, there's still some work to do to unite Democrats and move away from that Platner controversy.

We caught up with Jackson afterward and asked him about that.

ZELENY: Part of seeing the energy that Graham Platner brought without being consumed by the baggage, how do you do that?

JACKSON: Graham just tapped into, I believe, what was already there, people's frustration, you know, their anger that government was not working for him. This is not about Graham, it's about the movement, the people, the issues. It's bigger than any one person. I know for a fact it's bigger than me.

ZELENY: And as we talked to Jackson, he also told us that he would not support Chuck Schumer to be the Democratic Senate leader should Democrats win a majority in the U.S. Senate. But, of course, before any of that can be discussed, he must win this race. And that definitely remains an open question.

He said it is a challenge. There is no question about it, a fundraising challenge as well. Susan Collins has a big head start. The Democrats are all in on this race. They still see it as an important piece of the puzzle if they're going to try and win control of the Senate.

Jeff Zeleny, CNN, Bangor, Maine. BLACKWELL: Headlines we're watching this morning, a NASA astronaut is back on Earth after nearly eight months aboard the International Space Station. Chris Williams and two Russian crewmates landed safely in Kazakhstan about a half hour ago aboard the Soyuz spacecraft. It was the first space flight for Williams. He'll now begin post-landing medical checks before heading back to the U.S.

Gas prices climbing again as fighting between Iran and the U.S. intensifies. The average price for a gallon of gas is now $4.11 nationwide. That's up $0.11 in just the past week.

Renewed fighting has slowed shipping through key waterways in the Middle East, making it harder to move crude oil to world markets.

In New York, new video shows several teenagers riding on top of a moving subway train in Brooklyn. Look at this. Police say drones spotted six people on the train and alerted officers on the ground. Five teens were arrested, including a 12-year-old. Investigators say they recovered six stolen MTA keys from one of the suspects. The teens now face several charges, including reckless endangerment and criminal trespass.

Next, a high stakes meeting at the White House this week. What we can expect from the meeting between President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Plus, our panel reacts to President Trump ordering new signs at the Smithsonian Museum warning of, quote, "inaccurate information." That's coming up in the morning roundup.

BLACKWELL: This morning, CNN has new reporting about a key meeting related to the U.S. war with Iran. A source and U.S. officials say that Vice President JD Vance and Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine warned President Trump about potential consequences if he escalates the war.
